reader.title: Lynching of George Pfeiffer
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: The only account says Pfeiffer 'was hanged by lynch law' in Kansas and 'summarily executed' instead of tried (A2).

A2 reports a hanging 'by lynch law' after a confession made the courts seem useless, which gives a killing without lawful authority under a pretext of justice; it names no mob, number or place, and the report rests on letters and papers received in his Pennsylvania hometown.
Both articles print the same Lock Haven dispatch of Jan. 18, itself based on letters and newspapers received at Howard, Pa. (A1, A2); no Kansas report was found.

summary.text: The lynching of George Pfeiffer was the reported hanging in Kansas, around the turn of 1882, of a Pennsylvania-raised man charged with robbing the mails.
According to a dispatch from Lock Haven, Pennsylvania, he had confessed to mail robbery, arson and poisoning his wife, and Kansans, judging a trial useless, hanged him "by lynch law."
Pfeiffer, a farmer's son, grew up near Howard, Centre County, Pennsylvania, and married a Miss Reish of Brush Valley.

About five years earlier, the Howard house he lived in, owned by Rev. Nathan J. Mitchell, burned "under circumstances which excited suspicion," and after collecting the insurance on his goods he moved west.
His wife died in the spring of 1881, and he brought her body back to Centre County for burial.
In the fall of 1881 detectives arrested Pfeiffer at Driftwood, Cameron County, Pennsylvania, on a charge of robbing the mails in Kansas, and he was taken back to that state for trial.
Letters and newspapers received at Howard said he confessed to the officers holding him not only the mail robberies but the Howard fire and poisoning his wife for $10,000 in life insurance.

In the dispatch's words, the people of Kansas held that "it was useless to take up the time of the courts, after such a confession," and Pfeiffer "was summarily executed" a few weeks before January 18, 1882.
The coverage gives no town, number of lynchers or account of how he left the officers' hands, and no inquest is reported.
The dispatch closed by saying his career had "plunged two respectable families in to deep sorrow."
The Lock Haven dispatch, dated January 18, ran under the headline "Lynched in Kansas," in the Juniata Sentinel and Republican on February 1 and the Millheim Journal on February 2, 1882.

The Millheim Journal's deck, "A Pennsylvania Man Sets Fire to a House and Murders His Wife," stated the accusations as fact, and the text described the lynching as the "practical business view" of Kansans without criticism.
It named no race for Pfeiffer, and no Kansas account of the hanging appears in the coverage.

accounts.label: Lock Haven dispatch (hometown report from letters and papers)
accounts.gist: Pfeiffer, arrested in Pennsylvania on a Kansas mail-robbery charge and returned for trial, confessed to mail robbery, arson and poisoning his wife, and Kansans, judging a trial useless, hanged him by lynch law.

framing.detail: The deck 'A Pennsylvania Man Sets Fire to a House and Murders His Wife' states the accusations as fact and the lynching is called the 'practical business view' of Kansans, while the closing lines lament his 'lamentable end' and the sorrow of 'two respectable families'.
The Juniata Sentinel and Republican ran the same dispatch under 'Lynched in Kansas' a day earlier.

quotes: Intelligence has recently reached this place that George Pfeiffer was hanged by lynch law in the State of Kansas, a few weeks ago.
The practical business view the people of Kansas took of the matter was that it was useless to take up the time of the courts, after such a confession.
His career has plunged two respectable families in to deep sorrow.
